title: The Hoby treasure — Roman silver drinking cups from a chieftain's grave, Lolland, Denmark
language_note: National Museum of Denmark catalogue record in English/Danish; the cups themselves carry a Greek signature and Latin-alphabet owner's name (original_text_excerpt), not a regional-language literary text.
date: grave: 1st century CE (Early Roman Iron Age); table service made in Italy around the start of the Common Era
findspot: Hoby, island of Lolland, Denmark; discovered 1920, excavated by the National Museum of Denmark
original_text_excerpt: Signature on the silver cups: [ΧEIPI]ΣΟΦΟΣ ЄΠΟΙΕΙ ('Cheirisophos made [this]'); engraved owner's name: SILIVS.
original_text_note: The maker's signature (Greek) and owner's name (Latin) are the only inscribed text associated with this find; the cups' relief scenes depict episodes from Homer's Iliad.
reference_translation: A Roman silver table service (washing dish, wine bucket and scoop, jug, tray, two drinking cups) of Italian manufacture, buried with a native chieftain c. 187cm tall, aged 25-35. The cups are signed by the silversmith Cheirisophos and engraved with the name Silius — possibly Gaius Silius, Roman commandant at Mainz 14-21 CE — suggesting the set may have been a diplomatic gift from a named Roman official to a Germanic elite figure.
translation_source: National Museum of Denmark object record, as synthesized on Wikipedia (Hoby treasure).
notes: One of the best-documented and most personally traceable Rome-Scandinavia contacts in the entire seed corpus: a named Roman maker, a plausibly named Roman donor (Gaius Silius), and a named/identifiable local recipient context. Strong hero-demo candidate for Pillar 4 (artefact intelligence) given the vivid Iliad iconography.
